title: Smithtown: Contested Land and Native Rights
summary: Nissequogue people challenged Richard Smith’s claim to their land. Agreements recorded payments and retained rights; colonial patents then strengthened an inheritable estate and required English settlement.

why_this_matters: Land loss was a process involving agreements, contested claims, colonial institutions and restrictions on Native access. Read the actors, obligations and continuing communities together; a broad outline does not mean every Native right ended on one date.
introduction_title: Native homeland, colonial claims and continuing rights
introduction_content: Nissequogue people challenged Richard Smith’s claim to their land. Agreements recorded payments and retained rights; colonial patents then strengthened an inheritable estate and required English settlement.
history_title: How control of the land changed
history_content:
A Native homeland, not an empty estate

The Nissequogue River and the land around it were a Native homeland before they became Smithtown. The surviving documents do not tell a simple story of Richard Smith acquiring an uncontested estate. They record Native objections, overlapping claims among colonists, negotiated payments, and rights that Native people expressly retained. Records of the Town of Smithtown, Long Island, N.Y.

A Native leader challenges the taking of land

In the account attached to the May 4, 1665 deed, Smith acknowledged that Nassetteconsett, a Nissequogue leader whose name appears in several spellings, had complained at a court held at Setauket in 1664 that Smith had taken his land. Smith relied on a purchase from Lion Gardiner and an earlier transfer involving Wyandance. Nassetteconsett distinguished that earlier tract from land reaching the Nissequogue River, which he said remained his. The court advised Smith to purchase the disputed land if it had not already been sold. This account is preserved in Smith's own explanation, not a verbatim record of the Native complainant's testimony. Records of the Town of Smithtown, Long Island, N.Y.

Payments did not erase every right

The resulting agreement named payments including a gun, kettle, coats, blanket, powder and lead. Catawump asserted a share and joined the agreement for an additional payment. Crucially, the deed reserved specified rights relating to mats, canoes, eagles and deer skins for the Native parties and their heirs. Editor William S. Pelletreau later interpreted parts of this language as rights to gather plant material for mats and trees for canoes. The deed's reservation is primary evidence; the explanation of every term is a later interpretation. Neither should be reduced to the claim that Native people simply surrendered all connections with the landscape. Records of the Town of Smithtown, Long Island, N.Y.

Patents, settlement and competing colonial claims

Colonial government then strengthened Smith's position. The Nicolls patent required him to establish English families, making settlement a condition of the grant. A 1666 boundary agreement with Brookhaven again required settlement and promised sufficient land for Nasaconseate and his heirs. Meanwhile, Smith and Huntington disputed their competing claims. The 1677 Andros patent referred to the 1675 court decision against Huntington and confirmed land to Smith and his heirs on both sides of the river. These instruments helped turn contested claims into an inheritable colonial estate. Records of the Town of Smithtown, Long Island, N.Y.

What the records preserve

The change was therefore a process: assertions of ownership, Native resistance, conditional agreements, settlement requirements and decisions by colonial institutions. The records document promises to Native families as well as colonial acquisition. They do not establish when every promise stopped being honored, nor prove that the families disappeared. Read this landscape with the adjoining Native homeland articles, rather than treating the colonial town's founding as the end of its Native history. Vanishing Tidelands: Land Use and the Law in Suffolk County, NY 1650–1979

whereintheworld_content:
The shaded area on the map shows the Smithtown region discussed here. Its outer outline follows the present-day town, clipped to land, rather than claiming to recover the 1665 deed or 1677 patent survey. The patent’s named anchors include Stony Brook, Lake Ronkonkoma, the Nissequogue River and the Fresh Pond boundary. Kavenagh’s historical map 8 places those claims in relation to Huntington and Brookhaven. The individual agreements had different extents and retained Native rights; this regional outline is not evidence that all rights ended in 1677.
